title: Zechariah 14:1–11
context: The prophet announces a day of the LORD in which the LORD speaks of gathering all nations against Jerusalem. The city is taken and its people suffer the violence of conquest; half go into captivity, but the rest are not cut off. Then the prophet says the LORD will go out to fight those nations, his feet will stand on the Mount of Olives east of Jerusalem, and the mountain will split to form a great valley through which the people will flee, as they fled from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah (compare Amos 1:1). The location of Azel is uncertain. The LORD my God will come with all the holy ones; some ancient versions read with him instead of with you. That day will be unique, with light at evening; living waters will flow from Jerusalem east and west in summer and winter, and the LORD will be King over all the earth, the LORD one and his name one (compare Deuteronomy 6:4). The land will be leveled, Jerusalem raised and inhabited, and there will be no more curse. Many readers compare the Mount of Olives with Acts 1:11–12, where Jesus ascends from Olivet and the angels say he will come in the same way, though the connection is a matter of interpretation. The living waters are commonly read alongside Ezekiel 47:1–12, Joel 3:18, and Revelation 22:1, each with its own imagery. Readers take chapter 14 in historic, symbolic, and future senses: some see the oracle fulfilled in events after the exile and in the coming of Christ, some read it as a symbolic picture of God’s victory and the gathering of the nations into his worship, and some expect a future fulfillment at the Lord’s return. Each of these readings appears among both Arminian and Reformed readers, and the question of the millennium does not divide the traditions as such. Shared ground: Arminian and Reformed readers generally confess that the LORD will be King over all the earth.

verses.text: Behold, a day of the LORD comes, when your plunder will be divided within you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a day of the LORD coming when Jerusalem’s plunder will be divided. The city faces real loss before any rescue comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the day of the LORD bringing both judgment and deliverance. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as opening a vision held in historic, symbolic, or future senses.

verses.text: For I will gather all nations against Jerusalem to battle; and the city will be taken, the houses rifled, and the women ravished. Half of the city will go out into captivity, and the rest of the people will not be cut off from the city.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD gathering nations against Jerusalem, the city taken and half its people exiled, while the rest remain. Suffering comes before rescue.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty even over the nations’ attack. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse soberly, without dwelling on the violence of conquest.

verses.text: Then the LORD will go out and fight against those nations, as when he fought in the day of battle.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD going out to fight against the nations, as in the day of battle. God defends his people against their enemies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD as divine warrior (compare Exodus 15:3). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as confidence that God will act for his people.

verses.text: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s feet standing on the Mount of Olives, which splits to form a valley. Many compare Acts 1:11–12, though the link is a matter of interpretation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see vivid imagery of God’s coming that reshapes the land. Shared ground: both traditions generally hold the connection with Acts 1:11–12 with care, reading the verse in historic, symbolic, or future senses.

verses.text: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains, for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel. Yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people fleeing through the new valley as they fled from the earthquake under Uzziah, and the LORD coming with his holy ones. Rescue is pictured as escape.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the earthquake of Amos 1:1 recalled and the LORD coming with his holy ones (compare 1 Thessalonians 3:13). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as hope in God’s coming.

verses.text: It will happen in that day that there will not be light, cold, or frost.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a day without light, cold, or frost. The ordinary patterns of creation are changed by God’s presence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see poetic language for a day unlike any other. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as part of a picture of God’s transforming presence.

verses.text: It will be a unique day which is known to the LORD—not day, and not night; but it will come to pass that at evening time there will be light.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a unique day known to the LORD, with light at evening. God brings light where darkness is expected.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an image echoed in Revelation 22:5, where there is no night. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as hope for God’s light, held in more than one sense.

verses.text: It will happen in that day that living waters will go out from Jerusalem, half of them toward the eastern sea, and half of them toward the western sea. It will be so in summer and in winter.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see living waters flowing from Jerusalem east and west, summer and winter. Life flows from God’s presence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image alongside Ezekiel 47:1, Joel 3:18, and Revelation 22:1, each with its own imagery. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the living waters as a hope image of God’s life-giving presence.

verses.text: The LORD will be King over all the earth. In that day the LORD will be one, and his name one.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD as King over all the earth, the LORD one and his name one. His rule will be universal and acknowledged.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession of Deuteronomy 6:4 extended to all the earth (compare Revelation 11:15). Shared ground: both traditions generally confess that the LORD will be King over all the earth.

verses.text: All the land will be made like the Arabah, from Geba to Rimmon south of Jerusalem; and she will be lifted up and will dwell in her place, from Benjamin’s gate to the place of the first gate, to the corner gate, and from the tower of Hananel to the king’s wine presses.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the land leveled and Jerusalem raised and inhabited from gate to gate. The city is restored and secure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the exaltation of God’s city (compare Isaiah 2:2). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as hope for restoration, held in historic, symbolic, or future senses.

verses.text: Men will dwell therein, and there will be no more curse; but Jerusalem will dwell safely.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see people dwelling in Jerusalem with no more curse and in safety. Security replaces the fear of earlier days.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an image echoed in Revelation 22:3, where there is no curse. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as hope for a secure and blessed people of God.
